text: When enemy pressure is high, maintaining initiative through direct engagement can prevent further positional disadvantage and force the opponent to react.
Direct engagement is a viable option when friendly strength is not inferior, as expected combat exchanges are unlikely to be decisively unfavorable.
Strategic options with higher estimated value indicate a favorable expected outcome under the observed conditions.
Under high enemy pressure, flanking can be used to gain positional advantage and disrupt enemy focus, while still allowing limited or opportunistic engagements.
When enemy pressure is limited, flanking maneuvers allow time and space to improve positioning before broader engagement.
Maintaining a defensive posture is preferred when friendly strength is inferior, reducing losses and delaying engagement until conditions improve.
Engaging the enemy can be used strategically to shape the battlefield by weakening key units and creating opportunities for subsequent actions.
Maneuver-oriented actions are used to gain positional advantage and set favorable conditions for subsequent tactical actions.
Strategic decisions aim to preserve force effectiveness by avoiding actions that would expose units to clearly unfavorable exchanges under uncertainty.
